title: Orbital photoinduced Faraday effect in a lattice of conducting disks
authors: A. A. Gunyaga, M. V. Durnev
abstract: We present a theoretical study of pump-induced Faraday and Kerr rotation in a two-dimensional lattice of conducting disks. We propose a mechanism of Faraday and Kerr responses in which a circularly polarized pump directly induces a high-frequency Hall component $σ_{xy}=-σ_{yx}$ of the electron conductivity tensor at the probe frequency. Microscopically, $σ_{xy}$ originates from the third-order nonlinear response of the electron gas rather than from the real magnetic field created by solenoidal charge currents in the inverse Faraday effect. We show that the Faraday and Kerr rotation angles are significantly enhanced when the pump and probe frequencies are tuned close to the plasmon resonance of the disks, reaching $\sim 0.1^\circ$ per 1~kW/cm$^2$ of incident pump intensity in the terahertz range. This mechanism can explain recently observed giant pump-induced Faraday rotation in graphene disk lattices.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes the Faraday and Kerr effects in lattices of conducting disks, proposing that the rotation arises from a nonlinear, pump-induced Hall conductivity ($\sigma_{xy}$). The theory predicts significant enhancement of these optical responses when the pump and probe frequencies approach the plasmon resonance, successfully explaining large rotation angles observed experimentally.
main_problem: The study investigates the mechanism and magnitude of pump-induced Faraday and Kerr rotation in a two-dimensional lattice of conducting disks.
main_result: The rotation is shown to originate from a third-order nonlinear response inducing a Hall-like conductivity ($\sigma_{xy} = -\sigma_{yx}$), leading to giant enhancement near plasmon resonance, matching experimental observations.
method: The analysis uses a theoretical framework involving solving Maxwell's equations and calculating the nonlinear conductivity tensor ($\sigma_{xy}$) using time-dependent perturbation theory.
model_or_system: The system modeled is a square lattice of conducting disks (oblate spheroids) embedded in a dielectric medium, analyzed using a quasi-two-dimensional approximation.
key_observables: Faraday and Kerr rotation angles ($	heta_F, 	heta_K$) and ellipticities ($\epsilon_F, \epsilon_K$).
important_parameters: Plasmon resonance frequency ($\omega_0$), pump intensity ($1 	ext{ kW/cm}^2$), lattice period ($a$), and dielectric constants ($\epsilon_1, \epsilon_2$).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the low-intensity regime ($|\sigma_{xy}| \ll |\sigma_{xx}|$) and utilizes approximations for the current density and field components.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the photoinduced Faraday/Kerr effects, showing resonances in $	heta_F$ and $\epsilon_F$ vs. probe frequency ($\omega$) when the pump frequency ($\Omega$) is tuned to the plasmon resonance ($\omega_0$).
paper_structure: The paper develops the theory by deriving the nonlinear $\sigma_{xy}$ from the electron gas response, then calculates the resulting Faraday/Kerr response using transmission/reflection coefficients, and finally analyzes the resonance enhancement near the plasmon frequency.
why_interesting: The mechanism relies on nonlinear optical response ($\sigma_{xy} \propto |E|^2$) rather than the standard Inverse Faraday Effect, providing a novel theoretical understanding of giant optical responses in structured materials.

A circularly polarized pump wave induces a high-frequency Hall conductivity of electrons in the disks, σxy = −σyx, resulting in Faraday and Kerr rotation of a linearly polarized probe wave. The rotation is resonantly enhanced when the pump and probe frequencies are close to the disk plasmon frequency ω0.
